h1: Whisky portfolio tiers from regular to prestige
title: Whisky Portfolio Tiers Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: How Indian whisky portfolios are split into price tiers, what changes in the liquid and pack at each level and why tiers matter for planning.
teaser: Regular, prestige, premium, luxury: the Indian trade sorts whisky into price tiers. Here is what actually changes between them.
standfirst: Indian whisky companies talk about their portfolios in price tiers. New joiners hear the words in every meeting but rarely see what is different inside the bottle. This guide explains the common tiers, what changes in the liquid and the pack and why the tier a brand sits in shapes almost every number about it.
sections: The trade sorts whisky by price, not by style

In Scotland, whisky is usually grouped by style: single malt, blended malt, blended Scotch, grain. In India the everyday language of the trade is price. Brands are grouped into tiers, typically running from regular at the bottom, through prestige and premium, up to luxury or super premium at the top. Some companies use semi-premium or deluxe as well.

The names and exact boundaries vary between companies and research firms, so always check which definition a report is using. What does not vary is the logic. Each tier is a band of retail prices. Brands within it compete mainly with each other.

Most whisky in the lower tiers is a blend built mainly on extra neutral alcohol, a highly purified spirit made from molasses or grain, with a share of malt spirit, flavour and caramel colour. Moving up the tiers, the recipe usually changes in a few predictable ways:

  • More malt spirit and less neutral spirit.
  • Older malt, matured for longer in better casks.
  • Grain-based neutral spirit instead of molasses-based, in some brands.
  • Imported Scotch malt blended in, often stated on the label.

At the top sit Indian single malts and imported Scotch. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky explains the spirit types.

Packaging steps up with the tiers. Regular brands sell a large share of volume in small packs such as 180 ml bottles, often in simpler glass with screw caps. Higher tiers move towards 750 ml bottles, heavier glass, better labels and closures, then gift boxes at the top.

This means the cost structure changes too. In a regular brand, packaging and tax can dwarf the cost of the liquid. In a luxury brand, aged whisky and presentation make up a larger part of the cost. Our guide to whisky packaging cost drivers breaks the pack down.
Duty slabs can move a brand between tiers

Many states charge excise duty by price slab: the declared price of a brand decides which slab it falls into. A small change in the declared price can push a brand into a higher slab, raising its shelf price by much more than the change itself. The consumer then sees it next to brands from a higher tier.

So tiers are not only a marketing idea. They are tied to the tax system state by state. A brand can sit comfortably in prestige in one state and land awkwardly between tiers in the next. Pricing teams work state by state for exactly this reason.
Each tier does a different job in the portfolio

Tiers usually play different roles. The lower tiers carry volume. They keep the plants running, the distribution network busy and the company present in every shop. The middle tiers are where many drinkers trade up for the first time. The premium and luxury tiers carry more margin per case and shape how the company's brands are seen.

The industry often talks about premiumisation: drinkers moving up a tier as incomes rise. When that happens, revenue per case rises. So does the need for aged malt, better packaging and working capital. A shift in mix can change the whole supply plan.
Brands drift between tiers over time

Tiers are not fixed. Rising costs for glass, grain and energy push producers to raise prices. Over a few years a brand that launched in one tier can creep towards the next, especially where duty slabs amplify every increase. Inflation also moves the boundaries the trade uses, so a price that counted as premium a decade ago may now sit lower in the ladder.

Companies manage this drift in several ways. Some launch a new brand underneath an ageing one to hold the lower price point. Some upgrade the liquid or pack to justify the move up. Others hold the price and accept a thinner margin for a while. Each choice has knock-on effects on blending recipes, packaging orders and stock plans, which is why tier decisions are rarely made by marketing alone.
Tiers show up in your data in unexpected ways

Because tiers carry such different volumes, prices and pack sizes, averages across tiers can mislead. A rise in average price per case may mean consumers are trading up or simply that a cheap brand lost a state listing. Litres, cases and value can tell three different stories. Always split the data by tier before drawing a conclusion.

It also helps to know how a tier tastes. A guided, opt-in sensory session that compares a regular, a premium and a single malt side by side, with small measures, water, spit cups and soft drinks for non-drinkers, makes the tier names concrete for the whole team.
A first step for new joiners

Take your company's portfolio and place every brand on one page by tier, with its main pack size, the spirit types in its recipe and its top three states. Ask a colleague in blending or marketing to check it. That single page will answer more meeting-room questions than a month of dashboards.
faqs: What are the usual whisky tiers in India?
Typically regular, prestige, premium and luxury or super premium, though names and boundaries vary between companies and research firms.
What makes a premium whisky different from a regular one?
Usually more and older malt spirit, sometimes imported Scotch malt, plus better packaging. Regular brands rely mainly on neutral spirit.
Why do price tiers matter so much in India?
Many states set excise duty by price slab, so a brand's declared price decides its tax and shelf price. Tiers are tied to the tax system as well as to marketing.
